rules_text:
Rules summary Overview Have the most points at the end of 9 rounds Turn Pick a character to play, this character has a written power as well as a number to show initiative (lowest is first). If you play the same value then the omen card at the top of the board tells you who goes first. When it is your turn, you may take one land from the front row (the back row isn't available and is only to show what will appear next round). The cards in this row will slowly reduce as players pick, i.e. they are not replaced so if you are last you will have the choice of 1 card Each land scores points based on varying criteria on the cards: Farm cards (yellow) score points based on how many you already have. Forest cards (green) just score you straight points. Meadow cards (red) score depending on how many are in your realm and your neighbours. Village cards (brown) gain points for different land types in your realm. Mountain cards (purple) score if you have two and then four of them in your realm. River cards (blue) gains points equal to the initiative value of the character you played this round (max. 6) multiplied by the number of Rivers in your Realm. After all players have taken a land, discard your played character and draw a new one to your hand As well as the points on the land themselves, there is a variety bonus of 5 points for 5 different land types and 10 points for 6 different land types

[Rating: 2/10] Difficult to figure out who this is aimed at - it's too fiddly for casual play and too random for serious play, too much effort for a quick filler but not deep enough to dive in and explore. Feels like the design is pulling in all the wrong directions at the same time.

[Rating: 3/10] All six landscapes reward you for having lots of them, so the way to play seems to be:   Choose a landscape, whenever you can, draft that one. If you can’t do that, draft something you don’t already have, preferably denying an opponent. That way you qualify for endgame scoring and also gain more points when you’re forced to draft a hut (or if huts are your chosen type).  Finally, cross your fingers that you aren’t on the receiving end of too many hate picks. [Rating: 4/10] Pretty fun and gorgeous character art. Not sure it's worth playing in a pretty crowded genre but it's certainly fast enough that it just might be.

[Rating: 4/10] Vaalbara is a poor man's Libertalia. I really liked the idea, but the experience was extremely disappointing. Drafting the locations was boring and there was lack of variety in the card play, something that Libertalia never suffered from. It's probably better with more than two players, but at that point, why not just play the bigger and better Libertalia?

[Rating: 4/10] This is Libertalia but without the things that make Libertalia decently amusing, like passing around cursed relics, or murder.
